doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: Playing the white YMCA and who listened to the music
summary: The first black band at the white YMCA was told to play 'their people's music'; Carn reflects on white kids' knowledge of black music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What do you remember from your years — you mentioned that they weren’t ready for a black group. Did you experience, during your early music careers with being segregated from certain parts of your town or society?

Well there were a couple of incidents, but nothing that would break the spirit you know. I’ll tell you once we played at the YMCA downtown you know, so we was the first black band quote unquote to play at the white YMCA. And I think this was ’61 you know. And so — maybe ’62. So we played at the white YMCA so I’m playing white records you know, and the main thing was the Beatles, because the Beatles were the hot new thing you know. And some of the Beatles things I really liked you know. But by the time of Sgt. Pepper’s — you could say I was a Beatles fan but I liked some of the stuff they was doing. But the kids didn’t dance to any of it except when we played “Twist & Shout” and I was thinking that that was an Isley Brothers song you know — who was a black group — so they danced to that. So during the break we went in a little room they had for us with Coca Colas and fruit and sandwiches and stuff. So the director and a couple of the students came back there and the director said, “Doug, your band is very good and professional and it sounds real good, but do you think when you go back you could play some of your people’s music?” So the girl said, “James Brown.” And the boy said, “Otis Redding.” You know. And they started calling all these black group names. So I figured out what it was they wanted you know. So the director says, “Look, Doug, I could lose my job you know — I’m going out on a limb bringing a black group here and y’all are playing the God damn Beatles? Now you go back out there and play some of your music,
your stuff, like you know you’re supposed to do.” So we went out there and did [sings] You know you make me want to shout/shout. Oh they loved that.
That’s a great story. Do you suppose the white kids were hearing most of that from the radio stations or were they actually buying the records?

They listened to the high end of the radio stations. I figured they listened to their end you know? I even figured they listened to that stuff, but they listened to that more than they listened — now I knew who Ferlin Husky was. I knew who the Big Bopper was. I certainly knew who Ricky Nelson was, you know, and I knew who Tammy Wynette was. You know I knew these people, some of them, and, but they knew all our people. They were big fans of Sam Cooke you know. And so I never did figure that I was playing for white folks. I thought I was playing for upwardly progressive black people you know. And even when they got to be real serious deep jazz it was kind of the same thing you know, in the big cities and up north there was more black people into it per se. A great deal of the fans were white you know. And you know I found that really interesting you know, even to this day. It’s like that whole new generation, actually a third generation, in my case the white kids were into real jazz you know. So it was quite weighty and substantial in its substance, in essence you know.
